newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Milestone Bosnian election starts peacefully.
newsitem.headline: Milestone Bosnian election starts peacefully.

text.p: Heavily-armed NATO troops watched over Bosnia's first post-war national elections on Saturday but there was little sign of Moslem refugees venturing over ethnic lines into hostile Serb territory to vote.
Troops blanketed potential trouble spots along the de facto border between the Bosnian Serb republic and the Moslem-Croat federations. The start of the poll was relatively trouble free.
Federation Interior Minister Avdo Hebib said a single shot was fired from Serb territory at a voting station at Faletici near Sarajevo but caused no casualties.
"We are in full control of the situation on the ground," he told Sarajevo radio.
With thousands of people on the move, traffic jams in some parts of northern Bosnia were blamed on voters using their private cars to travel to polling stations instead of shuttle buses.
NATO spokesman Brett Boudreau said there were incidents but no systematic obstruction of people heading to vote and added:
"We would describe it and characterise it as a stuttering start to the transport plan, but there are no major delays. As to be expected, there are growing pains."

Almost three million electors were voting for a collective three-man Bosnian national presidency and parliament, a president and national assembly for the Serb republic and an assembly and cantonal administrations for the federation.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which organised the elections, and NATO laid down elaborate security precautions for refugees to return to homes from which they were ethnically cleansed during the war.
But there was little incentive for refugees to risk going back to their old homes since municipal elections which should also have been held on Saturday were postponed until November.

Arrangements were made for up to 8,000 Moslems to be taken by bus to the Serb-held Srebrenica area in eastern Bosnia to vote but only three men turned up at the departure point in Kladanj, a Reuter reporter said.
"There are not even eight of us to fill up a single bus," said 52-year-old Mehio Avdagic. "This is a big, big shame."
Srebrenica is notorious as the site of the massacre of several thousand Moslem prisoners after it was captured by the Bosnian Serb Army in 1995.

Only a handful of Moslems crossed to vote on Serb territory at Doboj in the north and the situation was similar in Brcko where a tented voting station was set up to receive any Moslem refugees who wanted to cross.
Thousands of Bosnian Serb refugees from what is now federation territory were taken by bus and train from neighbouring Yugoslavia to Serb republic towns in north Bosnia to vote.
One elderly Serb refugee from Sarajevo who had come from Belgrade said the outcome was predictable.
"Everyone's going to vote for their own family," he said in a reference to the nationalist parties that led the ethnic factions through the war.
The OSCE, which was able to monitor only half of the 4,600 voting stations admitted in advance that the election was unlikely to be free or fair.

The likeliest outcome was that it would consolidate Bosnia's partition after the Serbs openly campaigned for a separate state. Bosnian Croats are cooperating in the federation only under diplomatic bullying.

But U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke, who engineered the 1995 Dayton agreement that ended the war, was making an election day helicopter tour of Bosnia in support of the deal which was designed to hold the country together.
"The Dayton agreement does not provide for secession. We are opposed to that and we all agree that that is not what this election is all about," he told reporters.
Pitched against the prospects for unification are the ethnic animosities left by a war which killed an estimated 200,000 people, drove many more from their homes and devastated Bosnia's main towns.

One elderly Serb refugee was heard saying to a friend outside a polling station in Vlasenica in eastern Bosnia: "I agree. All (Moslems) should be exterminated for good. We didn't fight this bloody war so Moslems could vote in Bosnia."
